The organisation of the world's states, founded in 1945 after the Second World War to keep the peace and settle disputes by talk rather than war. It took the place of the failed League of Nations. Its charter was signed in San Francisco by 50 countries, and its headquarters is in New York. Today it has 193 members.

Every member has a vote in the General Assembly. Real power sits in the Security Council, where five permanent members (the United States, Britain, France, the Soviet Union, now Russia, and China) can each veto any decision. During the Cold War the veto often froze it. One exception was the Korean War of 1950, when the Soviets were boycotting the council and it sent an army under the UN flag.

The UN shaped the end of empires. It voted to partition Palestine in 1947, the prelude to the first Arab-Israeli war. It decided that Libya, made of Tripolitania, Cyrenaica and the Fezzan, should be independent in 1951, and ran the 1961 vote in which Southern Cameroons chose to join Cameroon. In the Year of Africa, 1960, seventeen African countries won independence, and most joined the UN that same year. Patrice Lumumba called in UN troops to the Congo that year. UN peacekeepers have stood between the two halves of Cyprus since 1964.

Its agencies fight hunger and disease, and it brokers deals such as the Black Sea Grain Initiative of 2022.
